newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries lower midday as auction awaited.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries lower midday as auction awaited.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were slightly lower at midday Wednesday ahead of the auction of two-year notes by the Treasury.
The Treasury will auction $17.5 billion of two-year notes at 1300 EST/1800 GMT.
The long bond fell 5/32 at 96-6/32 to yield 6.80 percent.

Early in the session the market received a boost from weaker-than-anticipated U.S. housing starts, which fell 12.2 percent in December to a 1.329 million annual rate versus expectations of an average rate of 1.470 million.

Phillips told a news wire that she would not necessarily wait until actual increases in the core inflation rate were seen before tightening monetary policy. She also expressed concern on the rate of growth and "taut" labor markets.

"Phillips remarks were just not well received and they're still hurting the market. She didn't say anything particularly extraordinary, but she did drive home the point that the key to tightening was not seeing inflation surface but economic growth," said Anthony Karadakis, senior financial economist at First National Bank of Chicago.
That was enough to offset housing starts data, he said.

Karadakis said trading volume was has been light ahead of the auction and that most dealers seemed relatively well positioned. When-issued twos were trading in the 5.99 to 6.00 percent range and many were hoping to see 6.00 percent at the auction.
"I imagine a lot of people would prefer to see a 6.00 percent coupon, but I haven't heard of any great demand," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Flanagan said the fact that the size of the offering has been cut back by $750 million wouldn't hurt supply, but that the amount of supply did cast an uncertain cloud over the sale.
"It shouldn't be a debacle or stellar," he said.
"At first we were up today, then Phillips brought us down, and then we went back up on the housing starts headlines," said Steven Wood, economist at BA Securities Inc.
However, the lift was short-lived as analysts attributed much of December's weakness to weather-related distortions, Wood said. The market has been "chopping around" since then, he added.
The Federal Reserve will release its Beige Book report of regional economic conditions at 1400 EST/1900 GMT.
"It's slim pickings" Wood said of the current dearth of economic data. Thursday will see the auction of $12.5 billion of five-year notes.

Next week two important releases were scheduled. Tuesday the Employment Cost Index was due and Friday fourth quarter Gross Domestic Product was slated for release. However, the Fed's 10-day "blackout" period also begins next week ahead of the FOMC meeting, shutting down remarks from Fed officials.

Separately, the dollar helped support the bond market Wednesday when it hit its highest level against the German mark since June of 1994 around 1.64 marks. The U.S. currency also remained strong against the yen.
The Fed intervened in the banking system Wednesday via a round of overnight system RPs valued at about $2.8 billion.
The two-year note was at 99-19/32, down 1/32 to yield 5.97 percent. In when-issued trading the two-year was at 6.00 percent.
The five-year was down 2/32 at 99-8/32 to yield 6.30 percent and the 10-year off 3/32 at 99-26/32 to yield 6.52 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.03 percent. Six-month rates were up one basis point at 5.11 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point at 5.28 percent.
